title: Der faule Heinz
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 164. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly (daß, gieng, Noth, heirathe, unnöthigerweise).
about: KHM 164 escalates one small refusal to work into a whole chain of them: Heinz, too lazy even to enjoy driving a single goat to pasture, marries the equally idle Trine so she can herd two goats instead of him herding one, then trades the goats for a self-tending beehive, then dreams of trading the honey for a goose that a not-yet-born child could mind. The daydream collapses, literally, when Trine swings a stick meant for that imaginary child and smashes the honey pot instead — and the pair simply shrug and go back to bed. The snail's closing line, that hurrying does no good, is the tale's whole philosophy in miniature.

sentences.t: Heinz war faul, und obgleich er weiter nichts zu thun hatte, als seine Ziege täglich auf die Weide zu treiben, so seufzte er dennoch, wenn er nach vollbrachtem Tagewerk Abends nach Hause kam.
sentences.l: Heinz was lazy, and although he had nothing further to do than to drive his goat to pasture daily, he nevertheless sighed when he came home in the evening after his day’s work was done.
sentences.i: Heinz was lazy, and though he had nothing more to do than drive his goat out to pasture each day, still he would sigh when he came home in the evening after his day’s work was done.
sentences.n: “obgleich” = although. “nichts … als” = ‘nothing but.’ “vollbrachtem Tagewerk” is a past participle used adjectivally, ‘the day’s work accomplished.’ “thun” is the 1857 spelling of tun (to do).

sentences.t: „Es ist in Wahrheit eine schwere Last,“ sagte er, „und ein mühseliges Geschäft, so eine Ziege Jahr aus Jahr ein bis in den späten Herbst ins Feld zu treiben.
sentences.l: “It is in truth a heavy burden,” said he, “and a toilsome business, to drive a goat like this out into the field year in, year out until late autumn.
sentences.i: “It is truly a heavy burden,” said he, “and a wearisome business, to drive a goat out into the field like this, year in and year out, till late in the autumn.
sentences.n: “Jahr aus Jahr ein” is the set phrase ‘year in, year out’ (German reverses the order). The angular German quotation marks of the source appear in this apparatus only as curly “…”; the t line keeps the originals.

sentences.t: Und wenn man sich noch dabei hinlegen und schlafen könnte! aber nein, da muß man die Augen auf haben, damit sie die jungen Bäume nicht beschädigt, durch die Hecke in einen Garten dringt oder gar davon läuft.
sentences.l: And if only one could still lie down and sleep at it! but no, there one must keep one’s eyes open, so that she does not damage the young trees, push through the hedge into a garden, or even run away.
sentences.i: And if only one could lie down and sleep meanwhile! but no, one has to keep one’s eyes open, so she does not harm the young trees, push through the hedge into a garden, or even run off.
sentences.n: “auf haben” is separable (aufhaben), ‘to have open.’ “muß” is the 1857 spelling of muss. The subject of “beschädigt, dringt, läuft” is the goat (“sie”).

sentences.t: Wie soll da einer zur Ruhe kommen, und seines Lebens froh werden!“
sentences.l: How is one to come to rest at all, and grow glad of one’s life!”
sentences.i: How is a man ever to find any rest, and take joy in his life!”
sentences.n: “seines Lebens froh werden” takes a genitive: “froh” governs the genitive “seines Lebens,” ‘to grow glad of one’s life.’

sentences.t: Er setzte sich, sammelte seine Gedanken und überlegte wie er seine Schultern von dieser Bürde frei machen könnte.
sentences.l: He sat himself down, gathered his thoughts, and considered how he might free his shoulders of this burden.
sentences.i: He sat down, collected his thoughts, and pondered how he might free his shoulders of this burden.
sentences.n: “setzte sich” is reflexive, ‘sat himself down.’ “überlegte wie … könnte” is an indirect question with the finite verb at the end.

sentences.t: Lange war alles Nachsinnen vergeblich, plötzlich fiels ihm wie Schuppen von den Augen.
sentences.l: For a long time all pondering was in vain; suddenly it fell from his eyes like scales.
sentences.i: For a long time all his pondering was in vain; then suddenly the scales fell from his eyes.
sentences.n: “fiels” is a contraction of fiel es, ‘it fell.’ “wie Schuppen von den Augen fallen” is a fixed image for a sudden realization — ‘the scales fell from his eyes.’

sentences.t: „Ich weiß was ich thue,“ rief er aus, „ich heirathe die dicke Trine, die hat auch eine Ziege, und kann meine mit austreiben, so brauche ich mich nicht länger zu quälen.“
sentences.l: “I know what I’ll do,” he cried out, “I’ll marry fat Trine, she too has a goat and can drive mine out along with hers, so I need no longer torment myself.”
sentences.i: “I know what I’ll do,” he cried out, “I’ll marry fat Trine; she has a goat too and can drive mine out with hers, so I need torment myself no longer.”
sentences.n: “weiß” here is the verb ‘I know,’ not the adjective ‘white.’ “rief … aus” is the separable ausrufen, ‘to cry out.’ “heirathe” is the 1857 spelling of heirate. “mit austreiben” — austreiben, ‘to drive out,’ with “mit” meaning ‘along too.’

sentences.t: Heinz erhob sich also, setzte seine müden Glieder in Bewegung, gieng quer über die Straße, denn weiter war der Weg nicht, wo die Eltern der dicken Trine wohnten, und hielt um ihre arbeitsame und tugendreiche Tochter an.
sentences.l: Heinz therefore raised himself, set his weary limbs in motion, went straight across the street — for the way was no further — where fat Trine’s parents lived, and asked for their industrious and virtuous daughter’s hand.
sentences.i: So Heinz got up, set his weary limbs in motion, went straight across the street — for the way was no longer than that — to where fat Trine’s parents lived, and asked for the hand of their industrious and virtuous daughter.
sentences.n: “erhob sich” is reflexive, ‘got up.’ “hielt … an” (anhalten), here “um jemandes Tochter anhalten,” the set phrase for asking for a woman’s hand. “gieng” is the 1857 spelling of ging.

sentences.t: Die Eltern besannen sich nicht lange, „gleich und gleich gesellt sich gern“ meinten sie und willigten ein.
sentences.l: The parents did not reflect long, “like and like keep gladly together,” they thought, and consented.
sentences.i: The parents did not think long about it — “like takes gladly to like,” they said — and gave their consent.
sentences.n: “besannen sich” is reflexive, ‘thought it over.’ “gleich und gleich gesellt sich gern” is a proverb, ‘birds of a feather flock together.’ “willigten ein” — einwilligen, ‘to consent.’

sentences.t: Nun ward die dicke Trine Heinzens Frau und trieb die beiden Ziegen aus.
sentences.l: Now fat Trine became Heinz’s wife and drove the two goats out.
sentences.i: Now fat Trine became Heinz’s wife and drove both goats out to pasture.
sentences.n: “ward” is the old preterite of werden, ‘became’ (modern wurde). “Heinzens” is an old genitive of the name. “trieb … aus” — austreiben, ‘to drive out.’

sentences.t: Heinz hatte gute Tage und brauchte sich von keiner andern Arbeit zu erholen, als von seiner eigenen Faulheit.
sentences.l: Heinz had good days and needed to recover from no other work than from his own laziness.
sentences.i: Heinz had an easy time of it and needed no rest from any labor but his own idleness.
sentences.n: “brauchte sich … zu erholen” — brauchen + zu, ‘needed to.’ The joke turns on “keiner andern Arbeit als … Faulheit” — no work but laziness itself.

sentences.t: Nur dann und wann gieng er mit hinaus und sagte „es geschieht bloß damit mir die Ruhe hernach desto besser schmeckt: man verliert sonst alles Gefühl dafür.“
sentences.l: Only now and then did he go out with her and said, “it happens only so that the rest afterward tastes all the better to me: otherwise one loses all feeling for it.”
sentences.i: Only now and then would he go out with her, saying, “I only do it so that the rest afterwards tastes all the sweeter: otherwise one loses all sense of it.”
sentences.n: “dann und wann” = ‘now and then.’ “gieng … mit hinaus” — the particle “mit” (‘along’) with hinausgehen. “desto besser” = ‘all the better.’

sentences.t: Aber die dicke Trine war nicht minder faul.
sentences.l: But fat Trine was no less lazy.
sentences.n: “nicht minder” = ‘no less.’ “minder” is the old comparative, ‘less’ (modern weniger).

sentences.t: „Lieber Heinz,“ sprach sie eines Tages, „warum sollen wir uns das Leben ohne Noth sauer machen und unsere beste Jugendzeit verkümmern?
sentences.l: “Dear Heinz,” said she one day, “why should we make life sour for ourselves without need and stunt the best of our youth?
sentences.i: “Dear Heinz,” she said one day, “why should we make life hard for ourselves for no reason and waste the best years of our youth?
sentences.n: “sich das Leben sauer machen” is an idiom, ‘to make life hard for oneself.’ “ohne Noth” = ‘needlessly’ (Noth is the 1857 spelling of Not).

sentences.t: Ist es nicht besser, wir geben die beiden Ziegen, die jeden Morgen einen mit ihrem Meckern im besten Schlafe stören, unserm Nachbar und der gibt uns einen Bienenstock dafür?
sentences.l: Is it not better that we give the two goats — which every morning disturb one with their bleating in the best of sleep — to our neighbor, and he gives us a beehive for them?
sentences.i: Isn’t it better that we give both goats — which every morning wake one with their bleating in the deepest sleep — to our neighbor, and he gives us a beehive in return?
sentences.n: “Meckern” is the goats’ bleating (from meckern). The relative clause “die … stören” is wedged between the goats and their destination “unserm Nachbar,” a very German bracketing. “einen … stören” — “einen” is the impersonal object, ‘disturb one.’

sentences.t: den Bienenstock stellen wir an einen sonnigen Platz hinter das Haus und bekümmern uns weiter nicht darum.
sentences.l: the beehive we set in a sunny place behind the house and trouble ourselves no further about it.
sentences.i: the hive we put in a sunny spot behind the house and give it no further thought.
sentences.n: The object “den Bienenstock” is fronted for emphasis (V2 puts the verb “stellen” second). “bekümmern uns … nicht darum” — sich um etwas bekümmern, ‘to concern oneself with something.’

sentences.t: Die Bienen brauchen nicht gehütet und nicht ins Feld getrieben zu werden: sie fliegen aus, finden den Weg nach Haus von selbst wieder und sammeln Honig ohne daß es uns die geringste Mühe macht.“
sentences.l: The bees need not be tended nor driven into the field: they fly out, find the way home again by themselves, and gather honey without its costing us the slightest trouble.”
sentences.i: The bees need not be herded or driven out to the field: they fly off, find their own way home again, and gather honey without giving us the slightest trouble.”
sentences.n: “brauchen nicht … zu werden” is a passive infinitive with brauchen, ‘need not be.’ “ohne daß” = ‘without (its being the case that).’ “fliegen aus” — ausfliegen.

sentences.t: „Du hast wie eine verständige Frau gesprochen“ antwortete Heinz, „deinen Vorschlag wollen wir ohne Zaudern ausführen: außerdem schmeckt und nährt der Honig besser als die Ziegenmilch und läßt sich auch länger aufbewahren.“
sentences.l: “You have spoken like a sensible woman,” answered Heinz, “your proposal we will carry out without hesitation: besides, honey tastes and nourishes better than goat’s milk and can also be kept longer.”
sentences.i: “You have spoken like a sensible woman,” answered Heinz, “we’ll carry out your proposal without delay: besides, honey tastes better and is more nourishing than goat’s milk, and keeps longer too.”
sentences.n: “deinen Vorschlag” is fronted before the verb “wollen” (V2). “ohne Zaudern” = ‘without hesitation.’ “läßt sich … aufbewahren” — lassen + reflexive infinitive expresses possibility, ‘can be kept.’

sentences.t: Der Nachbar gab für die beiden Ziegen gerne einen Bienenstock.
sentences.l: The neighbor gladly gave a beehive for the two goats.
sentences.n: “für die beiden Ziegen” — ‘in exchange for the two goats’; für can mark what is given in return. “gerne” = ‘gladly.’

sentences.t: Die Bienen flogen unermüdlich vom frühen Morgen bis zum späten Abend aus und ein, und füllten den Stock mit dem schönsten Honig, so daß Heinz im Herbst einen ganzen Krug voll heraus nehmen konnte.
sentences.l: The bees flew out and in untiringly from early morning till late evening, and filled the hive with the finest honey, so that Heinz in autumn could take out a whole jug full.
sentences.i: The bees flew tirelessly in and out from early morning till late evening and filled the hive with the finest honey, so that in the autumn Heinz could draw off a whole jug full.
sentences.n: “aus und ein” = ‘out and in’ (German reverses the English ‘in and out’). “heraus nehmen” — herausnehmen, ‘to take out.’ “so daß” = ‘so that.’

sentences.t: Sie stellten den Krug auf ein Brett, das oben an der Wand in ihrer Schlafkammer befestigt war,
sentences.l: They set the jug on a board that was fastened up high on the wall in their bedchamber,
sentences.i: They set the jug on a shelf that was fixed high on the wall of their bedroom,
sentences.n: “Brett” is a board or shelf. “befestigt war” is past passive, ‘was fastened.’ The sentence runs on into the next unit.

sentences.t: und weil sie fürchteten er könnte ihnen gestohlen werden oder die Mäuse könnten darüber gerathen, so holte Trine einen starken Haselstock herbei und legte ihn neben ihr Bett, damit sie ihn, ohne unnöthigerweise aufzustehen, mit der Hand erreichen und die ungebetenen Gäste von dem Bette aus verjagen könnte.
sentences.l: and because they feared it might be stolen from them or the mice might get at it, Trine fetched a stout hazel stick and laid it beside her bed, so that she could reach it with her hand, without needlessly getting up, and drive the uninvited guests away from the bed.
sentences.i: and because they were afraid it might be stolen from them, or that the mice might get at it, Trine fetched a stout hazel stick and set it beside her bed, so that she could reach it by hand without needlessly getting up, and drive off the unwelcome guests from where she lay.
sentences.n: “könnte … gestohlen werden” is a passive with the subjunctive of possibility, ‘might be stolen.’ “darüber gerathen” — gerathen (1857 spelling of geraten), ‘to get at it.’ The “ungebetenen Gäste” (uninvited guests) are the mice.

sentences.t: Der faule Heinz verließ das Bett nicht gerne vor Mittag: „wer früh aufsteht,“ sprach er, „sein Gut verzehrt.“
sentences.l: Lazy Heinz did not like to leave the bed before noon: “whoever rises early,” said he, “consumes his goods.”
sentences.i: Lazy Heinz did not like to leave his bed before noon: “he who rises early,” he said, “eats up his own substance.”
sentences.n: Heinz twists a proverb praising early rising: split as he says it, “wer früh aufsteht … sein Gut verzehrt” means the early riser wastes his wealth. “verzehrt” = ‘consumes, eats up.’

sentences.t: Eines Morgens als er so am hellen Tage noch in den Federn lag und von dem langen Schlaf ausruhte, sprach er zu seiner Frau „die Weiber lieben die Süßigkeit, und du naschest von dem Honig, es ist besser, ehe er von dir allein ausgegessen wird, daß wir dafür eine Gans mit einem jungen Gänslein erhandeln.“
sentences.l: One morning, as he was still lying in the feathers in broad daylight and resting from the long sleep, he said to his wife, “women love sweetness, and you nibble at the honey; it is better, before it is all eaten up by you alone, that we barter a goose with a young gosling for it.”
sentences.i: One morning, as he still lay in the feathers in broad daylight, resting from his long sleep, he said to his wife, “women love sweet things, and you keep nibbling at the honey; better, before you eat it all up by yourself, that we trade it for a goose with a young gosling.”
sentences.n: “in den Federn” — ‘in the feathers,’ i.e. in bed. “naschest” — naschen, ‘to nibble at sweets’ (du is ‘you’). “ausgegessen wird” — passive of ausessen. “erhandeln” = ‘to get by bargaining, barter for.’

sentences.t: „Aber nicht eher,“ erwiederte Trine, „als bis wir ein Kind haben, das sie hütet.
sentences.l: “But not before,” replied Trine, “than when we have a child that tends them.
sentences.i: “But not until,” Trine replied, “we have a child to look after them.
sentences.n: “nicht eher … als bis” = ‘not before … until.’ “erwiederte” is the 1857 spelling of erwiderte. “sie” refers to the geese.

sentences.t: Soll ich mich etwa mit den jungen Gänsen plagen und meine Kräfte dabei unnöthigerweise zusetzen?“
sentences.l: Am I perhaps to plague myself with the young geese and needlessly use up my strength at it?”
sentences.i: Am I supposed to trouble myself with the goslings and wear out my strength for nothing?”
sentences.n: “etwa” softens a rhetorical question, ‘by any chance.’ “zusetzen” — here ‘to use up, expend (one’s strength).’ “dabei” = ‘at it, in the process.’

sentences.t: „Meinst du,“ sagte Heins, „der Junge werde Gänse hüten? heutzutage gehorchen die Kinder nicht mehr: sie thun nach ihrem eigenen Willen, weil sie sich klüger dünken als die Eltern, gerade wie jener Knecht, der die Kuh suchen sollte, und drei Amseln nachjagte.“
sentences.l: “Do you think,” said Heinz, “the boy will tend geese? nowadays children no longer obey: they do after their own will, because they think themselves cleverer than the parents, just like that farmhand who was to look for the cow and chased three blackbirds.”
sentences.i: “Do you suppose,” said Heinz, “the boy will herd geese? children obey no longer these days: they do as they please, because they fancy themselves cleverer than their parents — just like that farmhand who was to go looking for the cow and went chasing after three blackbirds instead.”
sentences.n: “werde … hüten” is subjunctive of reported thought, ‘will (supposedly) tend.’ “Heins” is a variant spelling of Heinz in the source. “dünken sich klüger” — sich dünken, ‘to fancy oneself.’ “nachjagte” — nachjagen (+ dat.), ‘to chase after.’

sentences.t: „O,“ antwortete Trine, „dem soll es schlecht bekommen, wenn er nicht thut was ich sage.
sentences.l: “Oh,” answered Trine, “it shall go badly for him if he does not do what I say.
sentences.i: “Oh,” answered Trine, “he’ll come off badly if he doesn’t do what I tell him.
sentences.n: “dem soll es schlecht bekommen” — “dem” is a dative, ‘for him’; “schlecht bekommen” = ‘to turn out badly for.’ “thut” = tut (does).

sentences.t: Einen Stock will ich nehmen und mit ungezählten Schlägen ihm die Haut gerben.
sentences.l: A stick I’ll take and with countless blows tan his hide for him.
sentences.i: I’ll take a stick and tan his hide with a countless drubbing.
sentences.n: The object “Einen Stock” is fronted (V2 keeps “will” second). “einem die Haut gerben” is an idiom, literally ‘to tan someone’s hide,’ i.e. to thrash. “ungezählten Schlägen” = ‘countless blows.’

sentences.t: Siehst du, Heinz,“ rief sie in ihrem Eifer und faßte den Stock, mit dem sie die Mäuse verjagen wollte, „siehst du, so will ich auf ihn losschlagen.“
sentences.l: Do you see, Heinz,” she cried in her eagerness and seized the stick with which she meant to drive the mice away, “do you see, so will I strike at him.”
sentences.i: See here, Heinz,” she cried in her zeal, grabbing the stick she used to drive off the mice, “see, this is how I’ll lay into him.”
sentences.n: The speech tag “rief sie … und faßte den Stock” interrupts the quotation, which resumes with “siehst du.” “losschlagen” — ‘to strike out, lay into’; “auf ihn los” gives the sense of striking toward him.

sentences.t: Sie holte aus, traf aber unglücklicherweise den Honigkrug über dem Bette.
sentences.l: She swung out, but unluckily struck the honey-jug above the bed.
sentences.i: She swung, but unhappily hit the honey-jug above the bed.
sentences.n: “holte aus” — ausholen, ‘to draw back the arm for a blow, wind up.’ “unglücklicherweise” = ‘unluckily.’ “Bette” has an old dative -e.

sentences.t: Der Krug sprang wider die Wand und fiel in Scherben herab, und der schöne Honig floß auf den Boden.
sentences.l: The jug sprang against the wall and fell down in shards, and the fine honey flowed onto the floor.
sentences.i: The jug flew against the wall and came down in shards, and the fine honey flowed out over the floor.
sentences.n: “wider die Wand” — “wider” (with -e-) is the old ‘against,’ not modern wieder (‘again’). “fiel … herab” — herabfallen. “floß” — fließen (flowed).

sentences.t: „Da liegt nun die Gans mit dem jungen Gänslein,“ sagte Heinz, „und braucht nicht gehütet zu werden.
sentences.l: “There lies the goose now with the young gosling,” said Heinz, “and needs not to be tended.
sentences.i: “There lies the goose now, along with the young gosling,” said Heinz, “and needs no tending.
sentences.n: Heinz jokes that the spilled honey was to have become the goose and gosling. “braucht nicht … zu werden” — brauchen + passive infinitive, ‘need not be.’

sentences.t: Aber ein Glück ist es, daß mir der Krug nicht auf den Kopf gefallen ist, wir haben alle Ursache mit unserm Schicksal zufrieden zu sein.“
sentences.l: But it is a piece of luck that the jug did not fall on my head; we have every cause to be content with our lot.”
sentences.i: But it’s a stroke of luck the jug didn’t land on my head — we have every reason to be content with our lot.”
sentences.n: “ein Glück ist es, daß” — ‘it is a piece of luck that.’ “mir … auf den Kopf gefallen ist” — dative “mir” of the person affected. “Ursache” here = ‘cause, reason.’

sentences.t: Und da er in einer Scherbe noch etwas Honig bemerkte, so langte er danach und sprach ganz vergnügt „das Restchen, Frau, wollen wir uns noch schmecken lassen und dann nach dem gehabten Schrecken ein wenig ausruhen, was thuts, wenn wir etwas später als gewöhnlich aufstehen, der Tag ist doch noch lang genug.“
sentences.l: And since he noticed still a little honey in one shard, he reached for it and said quite contentedly, “the little remainder, wife, we’ll let ourselves taste yet, and then, after the fright we’ve had, rest a little; what does it matter if we get up a little later than usual, the day is still long enough after all.”
sentences.i: And as he spotted a little honey still left in one shard, he reached for it and said, quite pleased, “the little bit that’s left, wife, we’ll enjoy, and then, after the fright we’ve had, rest awhile; what does it matter if we get up a little later than usual — the day is long enough yet.”
sentences.n: “langte … danach” — langen nach, ‘to reach for.’ “uns schmecken lassen” is an idiom, ‘to enjoy (food).’ “gehabten Schrecken” — past participle as adjective, ‘the fright had.’ “was thuts” = ‘what does it matter’ (thut = tut).

sentences.t: „Ja“ antwortete Trine, „man kommt immer noch zu rechter Zeit.
sentences.l: “Yes,” answered Trine, “one still always comes at the right time.
sentences.i: “Yes,” answered Trine, “one always arrives in good time after all.
sentences.n: “zu rechter Zeit” = ‘at the right time.’ “immer noch” = ‘still, even so.’

sentences.t: Weißt du, die Schnecke war einmal zur Hochzeit eingeladen, machte sich auf den Weg, kam aber zur Kindtaufe an.
sentences.l: You know, the snail was once invited to the wedding, set out on the way, but arrived at the christening.
sentences.i: You know, the snail was once invited to a wedding, set off on its way, but got there in time for the christening.
sentences.n: “Weißt du” — ‘you know’ (weißt is wissen, not weiß ‘white’). “machte sich auf den Weg” is an idiom, ‘set out.’ “Kindtaufe” = the child’s baptism, held long after a wedding — the joke of the snail’s slowness. “kam … an” — ankommen.

sentences.t: Vor dem Haus stürzte sie noch über den Zaun und sagte „eilen thut nicht gut.“
sentences.l: Before the house it still tumbled over the fence and said, “hurrying does no good.”
sentences.i: Right in front of the house it tumbled over the fence and said, “haste does no good.”
sentences.n: “stürzte … über den Zaun” — ‘tumbled over the fence.’ “eilen thut nicht gut” — ‘hurrying does no good’ (thut = tut); the snail’s absurd moral caps this comic tale of laziness.

glossary.traf: treffen — to hit, strike (a target) (3rd sg. past; traf den Krug = struck the jug, not ‘met, happened’)
glossary.weiß: wissen — to know (1st sg. present; ich weiß = I know; the verb here, not the adjective ‘white’)
